displayQuote: There is nothing noble in being superior to your fellow man. True nobility is being superior to your former self

meta.title: Who really said "There is nothing noble in being superior to your fellow man. True nobility is being superior to your former self"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: This famous 'Hemingway' quote actually traces to an 1897 essay by ethics lecturer Walter L. Sheldon — decades before Hemingway was born.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is nothing noble in being superior to your fellow man. True nobility is being superior to your former self'?
meta.ogDescription: Popular quote sites credit Hemingway, but the line was already in print in 1897 under a different author's name, before Hemingway could read.

answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — a posthumous misattribution
answer.sourceLine: The earliest documented version of this saying appears in Sheldon’s 1897 essay “What to Believe: An Ethical Creed,” published two years before Hemingway was born. The “Hemingway” version traces only to a 1963 Playboy piece that Hemingway scholars doubt he actually wrote.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “fellow man” / “former self” — not found in any citation before the saying went viral online

source.excerpt: There is nothing noble in being superior to some other man. The true nobility is in being superior to your previous self.
trail: An 1898 printing in The Clinical Reporter repeated the line almost verbatim but credited it only to an anonymous “Hindu Proverb” — Quote Investigator ↗.

The Hemingway attribution stems from “A Man’s Credo,” a piece published in Playboy in January 1963, more than a year after Hemingway’s death; Hemingway scholar Peter L. Hays has argued Hemingway did not actually write it — Quote Investigator ↗.
The line still circulates today credited to Hemingway on sites like Goodreads and PassItOn, decades after researchers traced it to Sheldon — Goodreads ↗.
source.excerptNote: Sheldon’s original 1897 wording — “some other man” and “previous self,” not the “fellow man”/“former self” phrasing popularly quoted today.

source.rightsNote: Sheldon’s 1897 essay “What to Believe: An Ethical Creed” is in the public domain in the United States, having been published well before 1931. Ernest Hemingway did not write this line; the attribution to him rests on a disputed 1963 Playboy article published after his death.

author.name: Walter L. Sheldon
author.heading: Walter L. Sheldon
author.bio: Sheldon studied philosophy at Princeton and trained under Felix Adler, founder of the Ethical Culture movement, before founding the Ethical Society of St. Louis in 1886. He served as its lecturer until his death in 1907, publishing ethical essays and addresses aimed at building a non-creedal, non-sectarian code of conduct.

misattribution.heading: Misattribution history
misattribution.intro: This line is one of the internet’s most persistent fake Hemingway quotes — it was already decades old when he was born.

items.why: The Hemingway byline traces to “A Man’s Credo,” published in Playboy in January 1963, over a year after Hemingway’s death. Hemingway scholar Peter L. Hays has argued the piece’s vocabulary and opinions are inconsistent with Hemingway’s authenticated writing — Quote Investigator ↗.
An 1898 printing in The Clinical Reporter used nearly identical wording but credited no author, labeling it a “Hindu Proverb” instead — Quote Investigator ↗.
A 1973 speaker’s anthology assigned the saying to the Roman Stoic Seneca, roughly 1,900 years before its actual first appearance in print — Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest confirmed appearance is Walter L. Sheldon’s 1897 essay “What to Believe: An Ethical Creed,” published in Ethical Addresses two years before Hemingway was even born — Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: How a St. Louis lecturer became Hemingway
lead: This tidy maxim about self-improvement circulates constantly on inspirational-quote sites, always with Hemingway’s name attached and often paired with his photograph. But the paper trail runs the opposite direction: the saying was already in print, crediting an obscure St. Louis ethics lecturer, before Hemingway had learned to read.
The Hemingway version didn’t appear until 1963, in a Playboy feature published more than a year after his death by suicide. Even Hemingway specialists are skeptical he wrote it.
context.detailsSummary: How the exact wording drifted over a century
detailsBody: 1897 (Sheldon): “…being superior to some other man. The true nobility is in being superior to your previous self.”
1898 (uncredited, labeled a “Hindu Proverb”): swaps in “former self.”
1963 (“Hemingway,” via Playboy): still reads “previous self,” not “former self.”
Today’s popular version, pairing “fellow man” with “former self,” doesn’t match any citation researchers found before the saying spread online.
context.pull: The saying was already in print — crediting someone else entirely — before Hemingway had learned to read.
